short: Custom burger boxes from VPN Packaging in Vietnam give restaurants and foodservice distributors a hinged kraft paperboard format to assess for pickup, counter service and takeaway. The reference has a square footprint, tapered lower tray and a front tab that engages its receiving slot. Size review starts with the widest filled bun, the full height of the assembled burger and any wrapper that will stay inside the carton. Send both the everyday burger and the tallest menu variant so the lid clearance and closure can be assessed with a filled sample. The large outer lid provides space for a restaurant logo or menu identifier. Compare board, print coverage, packing format and contact requirements against the intended holding time and service conditions. Share the order quantity by design, delivery destination and target date for a project quotation.
sections: Specify the clamshell around the fully assembled burger

Custom kraft burger clamshells suit buyers who need a lid and tray joined by the same paperboard blank. The reference shows a fold at the back and a single tab at the front, so a counter team can load the tray before bringing the lid down. The square bottom provides a surface for the burger to sit on while the tapered walls create a lip around the bun. Plan the sample around those working surfaces and the clear opening inside the tray.

Measure the widest part of the complete burger after assembly. A bun diameter alone can miss ingredients that project beyond the bun or a wrapper folded under the base. Record the full height from the bottom bun to the tallest topping in normal service. Take those measurements across a few actual servings because staff portioning and recipes can change how the burger sits. Mark the dimensions as internal targets and indicate where your team needs extra room to lift the burger out.

Give each size a menu role. An everyday single and a taller double can share graphics while needing different clearances. A larger footprint creates room around a wide bun, while a taller lid changes how a stacked burger sits during handover. Compare both at the sample stage before fixing one dieline across the whole menu.
Check the hinge, front tab and counter assembly sequence

The open reference shows the rear hinge, lid panel and tray as connected paperboard. A crease at the hinge needs to move cleanly without pushing the lid forward. At the front, the tab and receiving cutout need to meet after the carton has been erected. Confirm their position with the intended board because caliper and scoring can change how much force a crew member needs to close the pack.

Run a simple service simulation. Have the crew open or erect the carton, load a representative burger, bring the lid down, engage the tab and put the carton into the outer bag. Watch for a lid that touches the bun, walls that deflect during closure and tabs that catch under a high fill. Open and close a few samples from the same batch and check whether the carton can be handed off smoothly at busy counter speed.

The folded carton also has to travel from receiving to the prep station. Define whether cartons arrive flat, preformed or in another agreed pack format. A flat supply can affect staff assembly time. Preformed case packs affect carton volume and counter storage. Ask the quotation to describe the supply method explicitly so operations can compare it with their current program.
Review hot-burger contact conditions and takeaway holding

Specify what touches the paperboard at the bottom and at the lid. An unwrapped burger, a patty with drips, and a burger wrapped in paper present different contact conditions. Include the serving temperature range, expected time in the box, and any side dishes stacked above it in a paper bag. Agree the food-contact side, ink location and any liner or barrier with the project specification.

Steam and grease deserve separate checks. Observe where condensation forms under the lid and whether the bottom softens near pooled moisture. Test the pack at dispatch and again after your usual pickup or delivery interval. Bring both the assembled burger and the same outer bag expected in use. If the buyer wants an opening for ventilation, review the location against print artwork, closure strength and the customer's handling route in a physical sample.

Provide the destination market and requested material documents ahead of the sampling round. The kraft finish in the reference gives a visible appearance for graphic review. Board grade, barrier and food-contact documentation depend on the construction chosen for the application. Set acceptance criteria with the buyer before using the quotation for a production order.
Use the lid as a clear print panel

Place your main artwork on the outer lid, oriented for the person who opens the tab. Ask the team to check how the logo reads on a carton presented at the counter and when several boxes sit in a bag. Keep critical artwork away from the rear crease, front closure and tapered side edges. Large black lettering on brown kraft is the illustrated direction and provides a useful starting point for a sample proof.

Compare artwork against the paper color. Kraft shows through the ink and can change the appearance of light colors or fine reversed type. If a chain has a brand-color target, provide the actual color reference and ask to assess it on the proposed board. If the menu requires a sticker zone or order label, identify the flat panel that can receive it without covering the closure or forcing staff to reorient the box.

Use a printed sample to check the logo at reading distance and inspect the creases after folding. If the same brand also orders paper fry scoops and carryout bags, supply the approved artwork and color reference together. Match the way the artwork reads on each format, since the substrates and viewing angles can produce a different visual result.
Set the case-pack brief for procurement and franchise operations

Foodservice distributors need a case description that lets buyers reorder by size and artwork. Include the proposed product model, finished carton size convention, units per inner pack, units per case, case identification and delivery destination. If the pack moves through franchise locations, confirm how cartons will be recognized at store level and how receiving staff distinguish the regular and tall versions from the outer case.

Ask procurement and operations to review the same sample before locking the production brief. Operations can judge whether cartons are fast to open and close, while purchasing can check how case packs fit the order schedule and storage layout. For an export quotation, communicate the quantity per artwork and any pallet or label requirements early enough for case sizing to be reviewed.

Have several filled cartons packed together in the delivery bag, using the typical order quantity. Inspect the bottom box, the access to each tab and the position of separate fries or sauces after handoff. The right case pack and carton size should serve the routine as well as the photograph.
Pilot the clamshell across a real order mix

Run a sample against three orders from the actual menu. Use a small single served at the counter, a taller takeaway burger and a typical meal with sides. For the single order, observe whether the tray gives the customer easy access to lift the burger out. For takeaway, put the packed clamshell inside the existing delivery bag and check whether the corners catch as crew lower several orders together. For the meal, assess clearance to its own fries scoop and sauce cup. The checks reveal whether one size can do most jobs or the menu needs two options.

Record the burger photographed for the sample comparison, the time from loading to opening, how the carton was handled and which panel was inspected. Take one photo with the front tab closed and another with the lid raised at handoff. If you ask for a dieline revision, point to the particular fit, lock or crease on the approved model and give any revised inner dimensions. This produces a practical sample brief for a purchasing team and creates a reference for comparing later delivery batches.
Send this information for a burger carton quote

Tell VPN Packaging whether the use case is quick-service counter pickup, a delivery menu or distribution to multiple venues. Send the filled bun diameter and maximum total height in millimetres, whether a wrapper is used, and what else sits in the same carryout bag. Identify any project requirement for steam release, grease handling, direct food contact and destination-market documentation. A short video of the current packing sequence can make assembly and closure needs easier to explain.

For costing, give the annual estimate if available and the first-order quantity per size and artwork. Include the vector logo, intended print panels, destination, delivery time frame and preferred case count. If you have an approved existing carton, provide its measurements and photos of the hinge, lock and tray. Ask for a physical sample to check fit, closure, paperboard and stacking before confirming the production specification.
faq: How do I size a burger clamshell for a tall burger?

Measure the loaded burger from the base of the bun to the tallest topping and include any paper wrap. Provide the widest diameter and height for each menu variant. Check the internal height in the sample with the front tab closed so a tall bun can be assessed in the final carton shape.
Can the carton be printed with our restaurant logo?

The outer lid is the proposed print panel. Send vector artwork, color targets and any print on the sides for dieline review. The proof should show crease and lock locations so important artwork stays visible after the carton is assembled.
Can this box be used with a hot burger or greasy food?

Share the planned contact, temperature, grease exposure and holding interval. VPN can review board and any barrier against those conditions in the quote. A filled sample and the documentation for the agreed materials are part of confirming the intended use.
How should we compare quotes for two box sizes?

Request the internal dimensions, carton supply format, units per outer case, quantity per artwork and sample scope for each size. Comparing those details helps purchasing account for counter assembly, storage and transport as well as carton price.

short: Custom French fry boxes in an open scoop format give restaurants a paperboard pack for serving fries, chips, wedges and similar snacks at the counter. This kraft concept pairs a low curved front rim with a higher rear wall and a tapered body. The rim makes the contents visible and gives the crew an accessible loading opening, while the front panel carries a restaurant logo. Choose the scoop geometry from the actual fry cut and target portion, then check how unused units separate at the prep station and how filled scoops fit inside the intended meal bag. VPN Packaging in Vietnam can review the serving application, paperboard, artwork and packing needs against a project brief. Send portion weight, fry length, holding time, direct-contact conditions, order quantity by size and destination so the sample and quotation can be scoped together.
sections: Size a scoop around the portion your crew serves

Custom French fry boxes in this format are open paperboard scoops with a low front opening and a higher backing panel. They suit foodservice buyers looking for a branded serving format with fast access to the portion. The illustrated scoop tapers toward a folded base and leaves a flat area below the front rim for artwork. The product brief should describe the actual fried item as well as the serving label on the menu.

A small order of shoestring fries can fill space differently from the same weight of thick-cut fries, crinkle cuts or wedges. Tell the sample team what cut you serve, typical piece length and the portion weight at each size. Include a photo of a representative portion on a scale if available. The goal is to check the fill line with real food and compare whether the scoop can be lifted without the portion shifting or spilling in routine use.

Decide how the portion will face the customer. A scoop at a snack counter may be held upright immediately after loading. If it will go inside a meal bag, measure the free height and space available next to the burger carton. The effective capacity and overall shape should be evaluated with the intended handoff method.
Check the curved rim, rear wall and loading motion

The lower front rim is helpful when a customer reaches for food or staff guide a portion into the open scoop. The higher back wall gives longer pieces additional support near the top. Compare the amount of support across sizes and check that the front panel stays high enough for the print to read when the serving is loaded. A narrow waist may look neat while leaving too little room for wedges at the base, so compare actual fills.

At the counter, trial the complete sequence with the scoop or tongs your staff already use. Retrieve one carton, open it if supplied folded, load the portion and set it on the counter. Watch whether the paperboard catches on the dispensing stack or whether the base needs extra attention before it will stand. Trial a shift handover as well if multiple employees use the same pack with different loading motions.

Set a realistic stacking expectation when the carton is empty. Confirm the supply format and exact nesting on the agreed physical sample. Compare loose, nested and flat forms with the supplier before specifying case dimensions. A storage-efficient supply format should also suit the time the crew has to get a scoop ready.
Evaluate the base and board with freshly served fries

Check the folded bottom with a warm food portion on the counter. Confirm that the base supports the loaded scoop and that the contact surface stays tidy through the planned serving interval. Use fries made with the normal process, since drain time and seasoning can change the amount of oil that reaches the paperboard. Record where oil marks appear and whether the scoop remains comfortable to handle.

Include serving and holding conditions in a material brief. Some buyers prioritize a matte kraft appearance and use the scoop immediately. Other buyers need the sample reviewed for a longer service window or a specific grease exposure. State the direct contact surface, expected time and temperature, and destination documentation requested. Paper grade, coating and contact-side requirements can then be reviewed together with the dieline.

An open scoop serves food without a lid. For takeaway, test the scoop in the actual delivery bag with the longest fries you plan to offer and a typical order of other menu items. Verify that adjacent cartons leave the scoop upright. A separate bag or tray arrangement may help keep a side order steady alongside sauces and drinks.
Make the scoop easy to identify by artwork and size

The front panel is the primary logo area. Keep the artwork below the front curve so the graphic survives die cutting and can be read on a filled scoop. Keep regulatory, menu or chain-specific information within approved print areas when it is part of the buyer brief. Use an assembled proof to check how artwork appears from normal counter height and how it changes near a fold.

When the range has more than one portion, differentiate them at prep and receiving. A minor visual marker in the supplied artwork, a case label or a clear distributor product code can help staff pull the correct size. Test that a team member can identify a carton quickly during service. If the packaging is part of a matching burger and fries program, check both products side by side under normal lighting.

Printed brown kraft changes the appearance of some colors compared with white artwork previews. Send a vector file and any color target you must match. Compare ink coverage and legibility on the proposed paperboard. If a selection is made from samples sent to several venues, record which proof and portion belonged together so the next order can repeat the same specification.
Plan stock rotation from the outer case to the prep counter

Ask for packing information by size. Cover the units per pack and per outer carton, the folded or erected condition, and how the units are oriented inside the case. For busy stores, decide whether the stack needs to fit a shelf, tray or dispenser. The size of a fully loaded scoop can guide the design, while the case arrangement determines how the staff handle stock.

Distributors handling multiple restaurant labels should state whether each case contains one design and whether a pack label is required. Provide warehouse labeling needs and quantities per print version. It helps to give a realistic first-order volume and how often the buyer expects to replenish, since a trial run and a repeated program can have different print and case-packing priorities.

If you plan to ship the fries packaging with matching cartons or bags, request dimensions and pack counts for each line item. Test a delivery configuration in which each line remains identifiable by the recipient. For a menu launch or seasonal print, confirm when the samples, approved artwork and packed stock need to reach the relevant destination.
Check the carton during dine-in service and delivery

Test the carton in the situations in which it will be sold. For counter service, ask an employee to load the fries with your existing portioning tool and hand the scoop across a counter. For a combo, set the filled scoop beside the chosen burger clamshell in the same carryout bag. For a delivery order, arrange the full contents in the bag and unbag them after the usual holding interval. Note whether fries spill into the bag or whether the taller pieces contact an adjacent container. These are practical fit checks using the intended service sequence.

Compare grease marks and packaging condition at the same points for each size and board option. Observe the rim, the common grip area, and the underside where the scoop sits on the counter. Record how long the scoop has held food, the serving size, and the bag arrangement. If the team needs a second sample, report the specific issue and which of the pack dimensions could move. Ask staff to compare the filled forms and purchasing to compare units per case using the same labeled sample reference.
Request a sample and a bulk quotation for fry scoops

Send the target serving weight, cut style, maximum fry length, preferred dimensions and whether the carton goes into an outer bag. Add the contact and holding conditions, any requested documents, and images of your current scoop or dispensing area material. Specify how many portion sizes you need and which require different graphics.

For the commercial brief, give the quantity per size and design, required arrival date and delivery point. Attach logo artwork and note the front panel treatment desired. Sample approval should cover fit with the serving tool, base support, brand legibility, case format and day-to-day handling. Ask for the quote to identify the agreed board, print and supply format so the order can be checked against the prototype.
faq: Do I order by carton dimensions or portion weight?

Provide both when possible. The intended portion weight explains the target serving, while a sample made with the actual fry cut shows the space and opening required. Give dimensions for the stock you use today if it helps establish a reference.
Can food counters stack unused scoops?
Confirm the supply format, whether erected scoops will nest and how easily they separate in a sample trial. Share the space available at the counter and the pack format you expect in the outer case.
Can we request more than one artwork design?
List each artwork as its own line with a quantity, portion size and requested timing. The packing and print proposal should make the versions easy to identify during receiving and service.
Is the scoop suitable for delivery orders?

An open scoop can be placed inside a wider outer food bag or meal arrangement. Evaluate upright placement, spill risk, grease exposure and holding time with actual fries and the same boxes or bags used in delivery.

short: Sandwich wedge boxes with a clear window from VPN Packaging in Vietnam are an option for caf├⌐s, foodservice distributors and grab-and-go programs that need triangular sandwich halves presented upright. The design shows a flat base, solid kraft ends and one clear window on the sloped face. Choose the wedge depth from the assembled sandwich, including the tallest filling and any wrap, and check where the bread edges and filling sit behind the window. A printed front band can carry the brand, with space reserved for any product or nutrition label required in the destination market. Send bread dimensions, filling depth, intended display time and temperature, artwork, carton quantity and delivery destination. VPN can review the board, window and tuck closure with a filled sample and provide a project quotation.
sections: Start with the sandwich on its cut face

A window sandwich wedge is a triangular carton with a flat base and a sloping front panel that shows the contents. This concept is for sliced-bread sandwiches cut diagonally, with two halves placed so the layers can be seen through the clear front. It is most useful when a deli, café or commissary wants to present several fillings in a consistent format across a chilled display. The bread and filling determine how deep the wedge needs to be.

Send the actual bread outline, slice thickness and dimensions of both halves after assembly. Show the direction in which the sandwich sits in the wedge. Include the distance across the highest filling, and note any wrap or liner present in the final packed format. A thick club sandwich and a modest sliced-bread sandwich can share a similar diagonal but require different depth and loading clearance.

Compare the appearance of a standard and a deeper profile using real portions. The edge of a taller sandwich may touch a slope or lean into the film if the depth is set too aggressively. A shallower filling can leave excess space in a deeper carton. Confirm the shape when the wedge is closed and standing on its base, then compare how the packed face reads from normal shopper height.
Place the clear window where the food should be seen

The sloping window provides the presentation area, while the surrounding kraft edges carry the printed design and give the panel its visual frame. Start with a photo of the sandwich cut face and note which ingredients the buyer wants visible. A physical layout can show whether the film opening exposes those layers after the sandwich settles in its normal position.

When comparing window sizes, account for where the film attaches and where the paperboard folds meet. A larger window shows more food, but the remaining paperboard around it still needs a printable area and room for the bond. Set the logo on the lower kraft band or another agreed panel. Verify that ingredient information or a variable date label has a clear zone, particularly if a sticker is applied after packing.

Review the window in the actual display. Consider fridge lighting, shopper viewing angle and reflections on the film. Check how a front label affects visibility and whether condensation develops in the intended holding interval. Set the test using the cold product, pack temperature and display practices that your team already uses.
Trial the rear tuck closure with the packing team

The reference wedge uses a rear opening for loading. The packer needs enough room to insert both halves and close the flap without rubbing the bread edge or disturbing the filling. Have staff load a small batch with the usual portion and compare packing time between a standard fill and the thickest planned menu item. Inspect the flap after closure to see if pressure from the contents makes it lift.

Confirm how units arrive and are made ready for packing. A flat-packed wedge can use less storage area before assembly. An already formed item may suit the speed requirements of a commissary or a different style of case packing. Trial assembly, loading and fridge placement as one workflow. Ask the quote to document the supply condition and number of wedges in a pack so operations can plan for shifts and stock rotation.

Observe what happens after transfer to the display fridge. Look at how the wedge stands when the cabinet is restocked, whether adjacent boxes press on the window and how easily a shopper can take one. The floor of the wedge and the strength of the closed rear flap should be checked on the same packed sample used for print and window approval.
Write the contact and chilled-display specification

Define the role of the paperboard and the clear film in the final food-contact assembly. An unwrapped cut sandwich, a moisture-rich filling and a prewrapped sandwich put different demands on the packaging. Give the planned range of temperatures, the time the product is held before sale and whether the window can touch a filling. Share any buyer or market documentation requests at the quotation stage.

Use the approved sample to evaluate what is actually visible during chilling. Check whether the film remains sufficiently clear for shelf presentation and whether the packed sandwich leaves marks at the corners of the wedge. Review the bottom edges, sizing and back flap after the intended holding period. Confirm the final materials and contact use with the agreed documentation before production.

Recycling, separation and disposal depend on the materials chosen for board, film and adhesive, along with the destination's collection system. If a customer needs a disposal statement on-pack, identify that requirement when setting the window material and artwork. Base the printed statement on the documented construction and market rather than the look of kraft paper alone.
Prepare the artwork and product information for a grab-and-go range

Plan fixed print and variable information in the same dieline review. Artwork shared across flavours can use the front kraft band for the logo and leave a consistent sticker area for a recipe name, date or product identifier. If each flavour has different colours, keep the format legible when packs are viewed side by side. Show the proposed position of the sticker and its precise size in the print brief.

Discuss printed areas on the front, rear and ends separately. An image rendered on a flat artwork file is read differently across sloping edges. Keep fine type away from window edges and ask the proofing team to check the assembled pack under shelf lighting. A buyer who needs traceability or barcode placement should include that requirement with the artwork and have the mark tested in the intended location.

Give a listing and case-label code to each wedge depth and graphics version. That helps foodservice distributors distinguish cases even when front artwork is shared. Confirm unit count, flat or assembled supply, carton dimensions and delivery units when you compare pricing between the different sizes.
Check the wedge through one complete retail cycle

Test enough packs to observe assembly, loading, label application, chilling, shelf replenishment and removal by a shopper. Load a regular sandwich and a deeper variant in the same sequence. Apply the actual variable sticker if one is part of the range. Arrange both on the intended shelf with other products nearby so the team can see whether the window faces the shopper and whether the label remains visible. Check the clear panel when loading and again after the planned display period using the same lighting.

Record the bread and filling used, the packed depth, the cabinet position and the window or label decision that follows from the trial. If a second sample is needed, specify whether the issue is film position, shape, label area, flap clearance or depth. Share photos of the closed wedge from the front, plus a view of the rear access, to provide a common record for the deli buyer, the design team and purchasing. The accepted pack should support consistent presentation with the actual ingredients and the workflow the buyer has approved.
Request a quote for your sandwich wedge format

Supply pictures of the complete sandwich, dimensions of each triangular half, maximum fill depth and number of halves per wedge. Include how you plan to load and close it, how long it spends in the display cabinet, and where paperboard or film will contact the food. Provide destination-country requirements, any sample label or approved artwork and an example of the display shelf configuration if applicable.

Send quantity by wedge size and printed design, target arrival date and location, preferred units per case and any transport constraints. A filled, closed wedge lets the team compare window placement, label readability and flap hold together. Review those points in a physical sample before confirming the production dieline and project specification.
faq: How do I tell if I need a deep-fill wedge?

Build and cut the fullest sandwich you sell. Place the two halves together as they will sit in the wedge and record the thickest part. Trial the pack closed and upright to assess panel clearance. Compare the sample against the thinner variants in your range.
Can the window placement be changed?

Share a photo of the cut sandwich and desired display area. The window outline can be reviewed with the dieline, margins, adhesive area and print panel. Approve those elements on an assembled sample before committing to a production layout.
Can the carton carry labels or branded print?

Supply the brand artwork and any variable label shape, size and print-panel preference. The assembled proof helps check text legibility and whether a sticker sits on the intended kraft surface without blocking the window or flap.
Is this designed for a chilled retail display?

Chilled, grab-and-go sandwiches are the intended buying scenario for this concept. Tell VPN the temperature, holding period and product contact conditions so board, film and closure can be reviewed. Evaluate a filled sample in the actual cabinet under normal lighting.

short: Paper delivery bags with seal are a branded carryout option for restaurants, commissaries and foodservice distributors packing closed meal containers. The concept from VPN Packaging in Vietnam uses a handleless kraft bag with side gussets, a flat base and an extended top folded over under an external paper strip. The strip is intended to provide a visible opening cue when the bag is opened. Confirm the contact area and the way the strip responds to opening with the actual paper, adhesive and handling conditions. Start with the widest meal box, the packed stack height and the headroom needed for the fold. Share the sealing workflow, order artwork, packing volume, destination and required documentation so the sample plan and quote can cover the bag and the closure together.
sections: Match the base and fold allowance to your delivery order

This paper delivery bag concept closes with an external paper strip across a folded mouth. The body is handleless, with side gussets and a rectangular base intended for closed meal containers. Restaurants can use the format to keep a branded order together through a pickup or driver handoff. The design brief should cover how the bag is filled, folded, sealed and carried during your actual service.

Start with the largest box footprint and the number of boxes typically packed together. Give the outer length and width of the lowest carton so the bag base can be reviewed around it. Record the tallest packed order separately and add the space needed to make the fold from a clean, unoccupied lip. A bag that fits the base can still be too short to seal after a tall order goes inside.

Provide dimensions in the order width, side gusset and height, with a sketch showing which side is measured. Show where drinks, sauces or labels sit relative to the pack. If the delivery menu varies widely, describe a normal order and the heaviest plausible order. Testing both helps the team decide whether one bag size can serve the menu or several sizes make daily packing easier.
Choose a closure process staff can repeat at pickup speed

The illustrated closure uses one fold near the top and an external strip pressed over the fold. The section of paper that accepts the strip needs to lie flat enough for consistent contact. Staff should have room to bring the opening together without touching the boxes inside and the strip should be easy to reach next to the loading area. Evaluate the motion on a full bag with the normal pack mix.

Show the existing handover practice if your team already staples, tapes or labels orders. Identify who seals the bag, how long an order waits on the counter and whether staff add a receipt after sealing. If a receipt or label is needed, designate a position that leaves the fold and strip accessible. Try the proposed workflow during a busy period or a comparable timed trial using the same number of hands and stations.

Discuss whether seals arrive separately on a liner sheet or are supplied in another format. Separate strips can allow packing teams to position them at the counter. A different application method will affect storage, ease of dispensing and the way defects are checked. Ask the quote to state exactly what arrives for the bag and seal supplies, including the quantity of each.
Check visible-opening evidence in the agreed sample

Tamper-evident delivery packaging is a buying intent. For this fold-over design, the sample needs to demonstrate what a visible opening cue looks like in your workflow. Compare the intact closure with examples opened normally, for instance a strip that tears or a visible change in the paper surface after opening. Define what the recipient and the dispatch team should be able to distinguish at a glance.

Test the seal on the exact kraft stock and any printed finish used near the top of the bag. Dust, grease, moisture and repeated handling can affect the contact area. Trial the application immediately after bagging and after the usual wait. Review the outcome after carrying the sealed order as arranged for your delivery route. If a buyer has an acceptance criterion for visible damage or reopening, document it and agree the evaluation with the sample team.

Also ask staff to open an approved trial bag the way a customer would. Aim for a recognizable change at the closure while keeping the opening routine convenient. If a strip lifts during normal pickup before the bag is opened, record where the problem begins and how the bag was folded. Use that observation to revisit the seal position, material pair or fold dimensions.
Fill the bag with the boxes and loads you plan to dispatch

Pack an actual order with the normal box arrangement. Inspect the rectangular base, lower corners and side gussets with the bag standing on the counter. Because the illustrated bag is handleless, confirm how staff, couriers and customers support it during pickup. Note whether a load shifts into a gusset, boxes tip against the sides or the bag needs support at the bottom.

Separate outer-bag conditions from primary food contact in the brief. A bag holding closed containers sees different conditions from one that touches an unwrapped food item. Share the planned contents, moisture exposure and any requested material confirmation. The review can then cover how the bag paper, inks and external seal are used as a system. Confirm any material documentation prior to production approval.

Orders with drinks and side dishes can put uneven weight on the base. If drinks share the same bag, describe the cup tray and where it sits. Keep the sealing zone clean and allow enough height above the load. Evaluate the full sequence before adopting any single bag dimension across restaurant formats.
Keep logo artwork and order identification clear of the closure

Use the main front panel for a restaurant mark or other supplied artwork. The folding lip needs space to move and the strip needs a defined landing area. During proofing, fold the bag and check the graphics again. Place the logo at a height that stays visible after filling, even when the bag bulges or tilts during a real handoff.

If each bag carries a branch label or delivery sticker, provide its size and placement preference with the print file. Some teams also need a plain space for order numbers written at pickup. Designate these positions separately from the glue or folded overlap. That makes the pack easier for staff to use and helps buyers order the same branding layout again.

Distributors can compare versions with different print requirements and quantities by branch. List the artwork, bag size and number of seals expected per shipment. Request outer-carton information and specify whether seals need to be packed inside each bag case or supplied in labeled units of their own.
Set up a dispatch trial for seals and box sizes

Start with the bag and closure positioned as the packing station will use them. Use a routine order to see whether the base fits the containers without skew. Then pack a tall order to check how much paper remains above the top carton for a consistent fold. For a third trial, seal the bag and carry it as a courier normally would. Inspect the closure after carrying and again after opening. Keep one intact sample beside the opened example for review by the buyer.

Record the bag size, contents, strip version, place of application and condition of the kraft at the seal area. Ask each participant to describe the visible cue they actually saw. If the body wrinkles before the strip is applied or the paper picks up moisture, note how the workflow could be adjusted and what a supplier would need to quote a revised construction. Keep the approved paper and closure reference together so the purchasing record describes the actual tested pair.
Send one brief for both the delivery bag and seal

Provide the width, depth and height of your largest closed meal boxes, packed stack height, heaviest expected load and intended bag closure procedure. Give the normal and longest expected holding times and who receives the package at pickup or delivery. Include a picture of the current packout if it helps show how the cartons sit in the bag.

For a project quotation, send target quantities by bag size and print version, logo artwork, destination and arrival schedule. State whether you need separate paper seals, minimum headroom for folding and any documented visible-opening criterion. Agree the sample checks for board, fit, load handling, sealing and reopening before signing off the specification.
faq: Does the strip make the bag tamper-evident?

The illustrated strip is intended to leave a visible cue when opened. Verify the cue with the selected bag paper, strip adhesive and fold in a physical trial. Share the required test conditions and acceptance criteria before approving the closure for production.
Can we customise the bag and order the paper strips together?

Share the bag footprint, artwork, preferred strip placement and expected quantity of seals. Quotation can identify the bag and seal components together and state how they will be supplied, packed and identified for the receiving team.
How much height should we allow for the fold?

Start with the top of the tallest packed meal stack and show the intended fold in a prototype. Set the extra height so staff can make the agreed fold while the boxes remain flat. Use actual service loads to check that the folded section seals cleanly.
Does it replace an open-top bag with handles?

Consider the handling route and what staff carry. This handleless concept suits a procedure that closes the mouth with a paper strip. A flat-handle bag serves workflows where a carry handle is needed, and the buyer can assess which format fits each order type.
